newsitem.title: UK: Plight of ex-Soviet air transport system continues.
newsitem.headline: Plight of ex-Soviet air transport system continues.

text.p: The amount of passenger traffic has declined substantially in recent years amid continuing anarchy in the former Soviet Union's air transport industry, the International Air Transport Association (IATA)'s area specialist Horst Herlemann said.

He told an IATA conference on Wednesday that figures collated by Russia's interstate aviation authority (MAK) show air traffic volume in 12 of the 15 states of the former Soviet Union (FSU) slumped to 89 billion passenger kilometres in 1995 from 156 billion in 1992.

MAK receives data from all CIS states (except the three Baltic Republics) but Herlemann said there was "no more reason to believe in the quality of post-Soviet statistics than in the quality of Soviet statistics."
From Belarus to Kyrgyzstan, the collection of aviation data was flawed, he added.

Under the old Soviet system "the plan was law and had to be fulfilled by all means including the manipulation of data. The mechanism of self-deception worked quite well, not only in the Soviet Union but also in its satellites," he said.
"MAK has repeated difficulties in verifying or even obtaining material from individual civil aviation bodies which are not efficient and, as one might expect, not very reliable," Herlemann added.e
Adding to this chaos was the fact that in Russia alone there were over 400 registered airlines and in the Ukraine another 150 although most of them did not actually fly.
"Gone are those happy times when Aeroflot's regional offices would dutifully report what the plan proposed." he added.

Since many airlines and airports were still organised as one unit and liable to be assessed for tax on the basis of any statistics they submitted, Herlemann said, "the chances of receiving honest figures are small."
And as air traffic control services were also assessed on the basis of flights reported, a similar problem existed there.

Thus the FSU operates a route system "which has almost no economic rationale,.....It is mostly arbitrary and still reflects to a large extent the Soviet organisation of domestic air transport," he said.
If market-based aviation is to exist in the FSU, this approach has to end, he added.
"Route efficiency has to be measured...and decisions to serve a destination based on unbiased market research.
It was impossible for every state of the FSU to have its own fully-fledged national airlines serving the world "or even the former union."
He added: "The last five years of aviation in the FSU have made it clear that this approach is extremely costly and the results uncertain. Solutions have to be found and quickly," he warned.

IATA sources says the FSU has inherited an elaborate aircraft inspection system but its rules and procedures are now frequently violated or ignored, leading to a serious decline in air safety standards.

With so many under-utilised aircraft available, there were many fly-by-night operators breaching flight regulations and intimidating inspectors (and their families) when they try to intervene. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
